claims.text: Chemical short-range order suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys.
SRO clusters act as strong phonon-scattering centers.
At high temperatures, SRO dissolution restores phonon mean free paths.
Competition between SRO scattering and thermal disordering produces a non-monotonic thermal-conductivity profile with a minimum near the SRO ordering temperature.
W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf and MoNbTaW are examples of refractory high-entropy alloy systems.
A fully disordered concentrated RHEA has high lattice thermal conductivity because static-disorder scattering is minimal.
Intermediate-temperature aging can induce SRO without causing long-range precipitation or phase separation.
Aging between 0.4 and 0.7 times the melting temperature, followed by rapid quenching, preserves an SRO state suitable for measurement.
SRO clusters are nanoscale scattering structures distinct from grain boundaries and precipitates.
Local chemical ordering creates mass and force-constant fluctuations that scatter mid-to-high-frequency phonons.
Increasing temperature breaks SRO bonds and increases conductivity by reducing SRO-associated scattering.
At lower temperatures, SRO scattering dominates and lowers conductivity relative to the fully disordered state.
The SRO-ordered state will have more than 15% lower thermal conductivity than the fully disordered state at the same temperature.
Upon further heating, conductivity will rise as SRO dissolves and may converge with or exceed the disordered-state baseline.
The proposed behavior is limited to alloys whose mixing thermodynamics favor SRO but do not cause macroscopic phase separation during aging.
Precipitate formation or dominance of grain-boundary scattering would invalidate the proposed SRO-controlled transport regime.
The cited evidence contains no direct measurements of thermal conductivity as a function of SRO in RHEAs.
The effect of SRO on the mechanical behavior of W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEAs has been identified as a future research topic.
In MoNbTaW, observations of edge-dislocation motion contradicted a prior model requiring local SRO breakup to initiate glide.
The cited mechanical evidence indicates that understanding of SRO-mediated thermal transport remains incomplete.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes aging above the disordering temperature to induce SRO, whereas the mechanism says increasing temperature through the disordering regime breaks SRO bonds. As written, the proposed aging interval is inconsistent with the claimed direction of SRO stability.
